extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, judges, and law students
extracted.subtask_description: Examination of legal standards governing (1) when and how letters-patent may be re-issued (and when a re-issue is void for fraud or over-expansion) and (2) the distinct statutory and equitable procedures for repealing patents in the interests of infringers, prior inventors, or the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commissioner's authority over re-issue
rubrics_metrics.description: Authority to accept surrender of an original patent and to re-issue it is conferred upon the Commissioner; the Commissioner's act in granting the re-issue is final and conclusive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts, when validity of a re-issue is attacked, are limited to the record of the original patent and of the re-issue to determine as a matter of law whether the re-issue is lawful; they should not inquire into extrinsic facts outside the record (see Johnsen v. Beard).

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-issue closes inquiry into inadvertence/accident/mistake (except fraud)
rubrics_metrics.description: A re-issued patent closes all inquiry into the existence of inadvertence, accident, or mistake in the original grant; after re-issue only fraud remains open for jury determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rule was held in cases such as Railroad v. Stimpson. Courts will not entertain collateral attacks on these grounds once a re-issue has been granted, absent fraud.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collateral attack limitation by infringers
rubrics_metrics.description: Neither re-issued nor extended patents can be abrogated by an infringer in a suit for damages or profits on the ground that the letters-patent were procured by fraud in prosecuting the application before the Commissioner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An infringer may defend by showing invalidity as to points in controversy (patentability or priority), but cannot collaterally impeach the patent on grounds of corruption or fraud in procurement; such fraud is a matter for direct proceedings by the government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reissue void if it misleads the public
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a re-issue fraudulently misleads the public it is void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the re-issue contains claims or descriptive matter intended to mislead, or extrinsic facts that manifest bad faith on the part of the patentee (or corruption by the Commissioner), courts may hold the re-issue void (cases: Aultman v. Holley; Swift v. Whisen).

rubrics_metrics.name: Expansion of claims beyond original implies fraudulent intent
rubrics_metrics.description: An expansion of the invention beyond the claims of the original patent is always ground for a presumption that there was a fraudulent intent to anticipate and cover subsequent inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such expansion is against public policy and has been uniformly condemned; when re-issue enlarges original claims, courts presume fraudulent intent and may bar the re-issue (see Fisher and cited authorities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fraud (actual or constructive) renders re-issue void
rubrics_metrics.description: Fraud, whether actual or constructive, renders a re-issue void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between (a) fraudulent procurement of the patent (a direct ground to set aside a patent), (b) fraudulent attempt to conceal the true nature of the invention (a defense under statute), and (c) fraudulent or deceptive omission/misstatement corrected by re-issue—each has different remedial consequences and may be treated differently by courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different consequences for types of fraud
rubrics_metrics.description: Fraud in obtaining a re-issue must not be confounded with (a) fraudulent attempt to conceal the true nature of the invention from the public (a defense under statute), or (b) fraudulent/deceptive omission in the original patent now corrected in the re-issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The first is a matter between the government and patentee (properly adjudicated by the government); the others concern the public or a defendant in an infringement suit and may be set up in defense; courts should treat these categories distinctly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three classes interested in repeal
rubrics_metrics.description: Three distinct classes are interested in repeal of patents: (1) infringers who practice the invention in violation of the patent; (2) prior inventors whose monopoly is denied or restricted by an antagonistic patent; (3) the general public whose free use of the invention is suspended while the patent is in force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different classes have different remedies and procedural requirements: infringers get defenses in litigation; prior inventors have special proceedings; the public requires procedures to secure repeal in the public interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringers' rights protected by defenses in suits (except fraud in procurement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Infringers may defend in any suit for violation of the patent by showing invalidity with respect to points in that suit (patentability, priority), but cannot plead fraud in procurement to collaterally attack a grant within the Office's jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The issue of corrupt or fraudulent procurement is a matter for direct proceeding by the government; infringers are protected practically by being able to show invalidity on the points in controversy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior inventors require special proceedings for repeal
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior inventor, to secure full enjoyment of his monopoly, must use specific statutory methods (equity bills, interference/repeal proceedings) to obtain repeal of an interfering patent; the Patent Office lacks unilateral power to recall issued patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically authorized by acts of 1790, 1793, 1836, 1870 and codified in Revised Statutes (e.g., Sec. 4915, Sec. 4918). Remedies may include adjudication that the applicant is entitled to a patent and directing the Commissioner to issue it.

rubrics_metrics.name: 1870 act requirement: prior inventor must obtain a patent before attacking
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the act of 1870, a defeated applicant (prior inventor) was required to satisfy the government of his superior title and obtain a patent before attacking an adversary's patent in court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 1870 separated proceedings: one to obtain a patent for the prior inventor (reverse the PTO decision) and a separate repeal action; this preserves the presumptions of the PTO's grant/refusal and protects existing patentees' rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reform under Revised Statutes Sec. 4918 — remedy for interfering patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Rev. Stat. Sec. 4918 any person interested in one of interfering patents (or in the working of the invention) may bring a bill in equity against owners of the adverse patent praying for relief; the court may declare either patent void in whole or in part or inoperative or invalid in any particular portion of the United States according to the parties' interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The judgment binds only parties to the suit and those deriving title under them subsequent to the judgment. Suits under Sec. 4918 are chancery proceedings governed by equity practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of repeal judgment in inventor-vs-inventor proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: In proceedings between contending inventors the question in controversy is priority of invention; the court may annul a patent in whole or part only insofar as it affects the antagonistic interests of the contending parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court may annul either patent as needed to secure the prior inventor the unqualified enjoyment of his monopoly; patentability of the inventions described is not the central issue—priority is.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural rules for Sec. 4918 suits
rubrics_metrics.description: Suits under Sec. 4918 are chancery suits: they require due notice to adverse parties, are brought in the district where the defendant resides or is found, are regulated by chancery practice, and judgment binds only the parties and their subsequent assignees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defendant is not compelled to file a cross-bill to obtain affirmative relief; no statutory provision exists for notice to parties outside the district; delays (e.g., five years) may indicate lack of good faith.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two special proceedings for repeal (prior inventors vs public)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two distinct special remedies for repeal: one to protect prior inventors (private bill in equity/interference remedies) and another to protect the collective public (public repeal proceedings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior-inventor remedies may result in extinguishing the rival patent as to the parties and awarding a patent to the prior inventor; public remedies aim to annul the patent universally for the benefit of all.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public interest demands immediate repeal where warranted
rubrics_metrics.description: The collective public is entitled to free use of industrial devices not covered by a lawful patent; an unlawful patent deprives the public of that right and the public interest demands forms of procedure that may lead to its immediate repeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because issuance of a patent exhausts the government's power to confer the monopoly, an unlawful patent blocks later lawful patents and harms the public; special public remedies are therefore justified (discussion of sovereignty vs statutory authorization).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on injunctions pending repeal proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: A junior patentee cannot be enjoined from suing under his patent on the mere motion of the prior patentee pending a suit to cancel the junior patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, where a court annuls a patent, it may enjoin the patentee from instituting actions thereon; courts have discretion regarding injunctions depending on circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laches and timing: delay can show want of good faith
rubrics_metrics.description: A significant delay (example given: five years) in instituting proceedings to annul a patent tends to show a want of good faith in the petitioner and may be a factor against relief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timing and promptness in bringing repeal suits are relevant equity considerations; undue delay can prejudice the petitioner's case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on who may bring a private suit to annul
rubrics_metrics.description: No private suit to annul a patent can be brought unless statutory prerequisites are present (e.g., two outstanding interfering patents, or a refusal by the Commissioner or court upon appeal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have held suits to defeat another's patent cannot be brought until the plaintiff has his own patent where required; statutory provisions (e.g., Sec. 4918 and later acts) and precedent define precise prerequisites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judgment binding effect limited to parties and subsequent assignees
rubrics_metrics.description: A judgment annulling an interfering patent binds only the parties to the suit and those deriving title from or under them subsequent to rendition of the judgment; it does not affect unrelated third parties' rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thus a court's repeal in a private suit does not universally cancel a patent for all the world—public repeal remedies differ in this respect.
